# Every MCP server's tools, on the record.

Your AI client trusts the tool descriptions an MCP server sends it — and a server can change them after you approved it. HISTOR keeps a public, signed record of what every remote MCP server in the official registry advertised, and tells you the day it changed.

Remote endpoints: it lists tools and never calls one. Registry packages: bounded canary calls run inside the isolated sandbox. It never says a server is safe — it tells you what was said, and when.

What HISTOR is for

## Tool descriptions are instructions. They should not change behind your back.

The problem

### A server can change what your model reads

When you connect an MCP server, its tool descriptions go straight to the model as instructions. A server can pass your review with harmless descriptions and change them next week — one added sentence is all a prompt injection needs, and most clients never ask you again.

What HISTOR does

### It keeps the public record

Every day HISTOR reads what each remote (streamable-HTTP) endpoint in the official MCP registry advertises, fingerprints it, signs what it saw and appends it to a log that can only grow. When a server's definitions change, the change gets a date and a diff.

What you get

### A second pair of eyes you can check

Look up any server before you trust it. Paste what your client received and learn whether everyone else sees the same thing. Follow changes in a feed, or put a badge in your README. Every answer is signed, so you can verify it instead of believing it.

### Who it is for

People who use MCP servers in Claude, Cursor or any client — check a server before you connect it, and again when it changes.

Agent builders whose agents connect to servers on their own — call /check before trusting a tool set.

Registries and directories that want more than stars and download counts — show when a listing's tools last changed.

Server authors who want to show a stable, documented history — add the badge, and every change you ship is dated in public.

### Four words used on this page

Tool definitions
    The name, description and input schema of each tool a server offers — the text your model reads.

Pinned
    HISTOR has recorded a fingerprint (digest) of the exact definitions it saw, so any later change is detectable.

Label
    One signed statement about one observation: what was seen, what matched, whether it changed. Anyone can verify it offline.

Signed tree head
    The log's signed summary after each crawl. Comparing two of them proves nothing was deleted or rewritten in between.

Servers Changes Log Check Watch State of MCP

Read → digest → label → append → sign → compare

## How the log works

Six steps, every one of them checkable by someone who does not trust HISTOR. The only thing you have to take on faith is that the observation happened when the label says it did — and the log makes it impossible to change that story afterwards.

01

### Read

Remote endpoints in the official MCP registry: initialize, then tools/list, drained across every page; no tool is called, and private addresses are refused before the connection opens. npm and PyPI packages: installed and started in the sandbox described below, with no route out.

02

### Digest

The tool set is reduced to name, description, input and output schema, sorted by UTF-16 code units and hashed over its RFC 8785 canonical form. Anyone holding the same tools gets the same digest — which is what makes a comparison possible.

03

### Label

Four MTL/1 methods, one signed AWR/2 document each: what was observed, what the WARDEN pattern set matched, whether the definitions changed since the last label, and whether the name is on a threat list. No score, ever.

04

### Append

Every label becomes a leaf of an RFC 9162 Merkle tree: leaf hash = SHA-256(0x00 ‖ JCS(label)). The label you download is the leaf input, so you can recompute its hash yourself.

05

### Sign

After each crawl HISTOR signs a tree head: the size and the root. Keep yesterday's head; ask for a consistency proof to today's; if anything was removed or rewritten, the proof fails.

06

### Compare

Each day a continuity label compares the new digest with the last one. Equal: "unchanged since". Different: a change, with the date and a per-tool diff. A client that checks what it received adds the view no crawler has.

Where an npm or PyPI package is run

## Test conditions

A package observation is true for these conditions, and no others. Every package page names the exact image it ran in and any configuration it was given.

### System

Linux x86_64, inside gVisor (runsc): the package talks to a kernel written for sandboxing, not to the host's. An unprivileged user, no capabilities, a read-only root.

### Runtimes

npm packages in histor-node:22, PyPI packages in histor-python:3.12: the official node:22-bookworm-slim and python:3.12-slim images plus bash, git, Python 3 or Node 22 and a Java 21 runtime — never Docker — built when a sandbox host is installed. A package whose Requires-Python excludes 3.12 runs on histor-python:3.13 or 3.14; one that requires a newer Node runs again on histor-node:24. The exact image a package ran in is on its page.

### Install

npm with --ignore-scripts, then the install scripts in a traced stage of their own. PyPI: wheels only — a package that ships only source is reported, never built.

### Network

No route out. Every name the package looks up resolves to HISTOR's own traps, which record what was sent and forward nothing. A server that needs the internet to start shows that here.

### Secrets

None are real. Decoy credentials sit in HOME and a decoy .env in the working directory. A variable the package says it needs gets a placeholder; where the placeholder was sent is recorded.

### Limits

512 MB of memory, one CPU, 64 MB of /tmp. 360 s to install, 150 s to start and answer; up to 15 tools called once each with canary arguments, 8 s per call.

### Configuration

Only names: required variables its registry entry declares or that it printed when it exited, and a start argument such as serve when its usage text offers one. Never a value from anyone else.

## What a label does not say

The profile HISTOR implements forbids the words safe, secure, audited, certified, approved and trusted. Here is why, in the terms of what the log can and cannot show.

### Not a safety rating

A pattern match is a reason to read a definition, not a finding. Three of the four methods can never return fail. There is no score to rank by, because no score HISTOR could compute would mean what a reader takes it to mean.

### Not the code

Labels are about advertised text. A remote endpoint's source is never read and its tools are never invoked; a package runs only in the sandbox, against nothing real. A server can keep identical definitions and behave differently for real users; the log cannot see that, and says so inside every label.

### A change is not an accusation

A version bump changes definitions too. A change is shown as a date and a diff, in amber, never red. What you do with it is yours: re-read, re-approve, or pin the old digest.

### A package as run here, not on your machine

An npm or PyPI server is observed under the test conditions above: Linux, no internet, placeholder keys. One that needs Windows, a real account or the network may show fewer tools or none; its page says why it exited.

### One operator, one key

Today one party runs the log. A second observer on another network is the next step, and any AIMarket hub can run one. Until then, what the key proves is who said it — not that it is true.

### Behind a login, unseen

Endpoints that require authentication answer 401 to everyone without a key, including HISTOR. They are counted and listed as not observed, never dropped from the numbers.

Other logs, the same servers

## Outside checks

HISTOR is not the only public record of MCP tool definitions. Where another log publishes its reads, the two are compared on the same servers and days, and the result is published both ways, with HISTOR's own misses.

### ScraperWatch

A daily diff of a fixed panel of about 3,000 remote endpoints. HISTOR compares each of their published days with its own reads, and ScraperWatch shows the result on its page under "Outside check". The first comparison found a robots.txt parsing limit on their side and a handshake regression on HISTOR's; both were fixed the same day.

scraperwatch.com/mcp-changes
/datasets/peers/scraperwatch/latest

### heldfast

An open daily record of the tool definitions of the servers in the official MCP registry. Of the 23,190 servers both logs recorded on 26 October 2026, 21,215 had every field in both; on those, 97.9% of servers and 99.1% of tools were identical byte for byte, and each difference has a stated cause: package versions, read times, failed reads, a first page only, an older protocol.

For clients, registries and server authors

## Use it

Before your agent trusts a server, send the tools it received. The answer is signed by the log's did:key and names the tree head it was given under.
    
    curl -sS https://histor.modelmarket.dev/api/v1/check \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"endpoint":"https://example.com/mcp","tools":[ …tools/list result… ],"contribute":true}'
    # -> {"type":"histor.check/v1","match":"same"|"different"|"previously-observed"|…,
    #     "observed":{"unchangedSince":"…","changes":0}, "patternScan":{…}, "signature":{…}}
    
    # README badge for your server
    [![MCP tool defs](https://histor.modelmarket.dev/badge/<id>.svg)](https://histor.modelmarket.dev/s/<id>)
    
    # Atom feed of every observed change
    https://histor.modelmarket.dev/feed.xml

## Questions

Is this a marketplace listing?

No. The server list is the log's index: every remote endpoint in the official MCP registry, with what HISTOR could observe about it. Nothing here is for sale and nothing is ranked by quality.

Does HISTOR tell me a server is safe?

No, and it never will. It tells you what a server advertised, whether that changed, and which published patterns matched the text. Whether to trust the server is your decision — HISTOR makes sure you decide on the same facts as everyone else.

Why are so many servers "not observed"?

Most remote MCP endpoints require a login (they answer 401 to anyone without a key), some use the legacy SSE transport or need per-user values in the URL, and some are simply down. They stay on the list with the reason, so the numbers never hide them.

How do I check a server I already use?

Open the Check tab, paste the server's endpoint and the tools/list result your client received, and press Check. You get back, signed, whether HISTOR observed the same definitions — or different ones, or an older set.

How do I get a badge for my server?

Find your endpoint on the Servers tab, open it, and copy the Markdown snippet under the facts. The badge shows the date your definitions were pinned or last changed, and links to the full history.

Why should I trust HISTOR itself?

You do not have to. Every label and every tree head is signed with one published key; the Log tab proves in your browser that the log only grew; and the command-line auditor does the same from any machine. What remains is that one operator runs it today — a second, independent observer is the next step.

What does it cost?

Looking things up, the badges, the feed and /check are free. HISTOR also offers histor.check@v1 to the AIMarket Hub, so agents can reach it through the market.

I run an MCP server. What does HISTOR send it, and how do I opt out?

Every 6 hours, and every 30 minutes for a week once its tools have changed twice in a week. First it reads /robots.txt (RFC 9309, product token histor, about once a day per site): a path that file does not allow HISTOR is not read, and its page here says so. Otherwise server/discover and tools/list (MCP 2026-07-28), or, for a server without that, initialize, notifications/initialized and tools/list — never a tool call, never a redirect followed on the MCP path, at most two connections per host, from a User-Agent that starts with histor/. To keep HISTOR out, disallow your MCP path for User-agent: histor (or for all crawlers); to let HISTOR alone in, add User-agent: histor with an Allow line for that path. An issue on the histor repository with your endpoint or host also works: it is then listed as not observed (operator-opt-out), with the reason, rather than silently dropped. Labels already in the log stay: the log only grows.

HISTOR

# We stopped reading 2,195 MCP servers for three days. Another team's log is how we found out

data monitoringloggingmcp serversserver managementteam collaboration

Read the full article on dev.toImage: We stopped reading 2,195 MCP servers for three days. Another team's log is how we found out

## TL;DR

HISTOR, a tool reading MCP servers, stopped receiving data from 2,195 servers for three days. This failure went undetected until an overlapping log revealed the issue. The article discusses the technical causes and offers insights for MCP client development.

## Key points

  * HISTOR's failure went unnoticed due to high success rates in server reads, obscuring the 2,195 inactive servers.
  * The MCP revision changed the session initiation process, leading to compatibility issues.
  * A new logging tool, ScraperWatch, helped detect the problem by contrasting its findings with HISTOR's.

## Quick facts

Affected Servers
    2,195

Fix Implemented
    November 1 at 08:44:57 UTC

Success Rate Before Fix
    98.8% on 9,514 reads

Protocol Speaking Servers
    19% spoke the new protocol as of November 1

Comparison Tool
    ScraperWatch

## Why it matters

This scenario highlights the importance of effective logging and monitoring systems in tech environments, demonstrating how overlapping data sources can reveal issues that otherwise remain hidden. It serves as a lesson for developers about backward compatibility and the need for robust error handling in clients.

## Who it's for

Developers and engineers working with MCP clients and network protocol systems should find this article particularly relevant.

## FAQ

What caused the disruption in server reads?

A change in the MCP session initiation process led to compatibility issues, causing HISTOR to fail in reading data from 2,195 servers.

How was the problem eventually detected?

The issue was identified by comparing logs from HISTOR with a new log system called ScraperWatch, which showed discrepancies.

What actions were taken to resolve the issue?

The reading system was updated to better handle protocol versions and errors, allowing it to recover from the failure.
